title: Eleven payment gateways, roles, usage billing and more
summary: Connect eight more payment gateways, give your team custom roles, bill usage with more pricing models, and get more control over collections.
body:
You can now collect through 11 payment gateways. This release also adds custom roles, a request
log, more ways to price usage and more control over collections.

- **Eight more payment gateways.** Square, Braintree, Checkout.com, Adyen, Mollie, Authorize.net,
  GoCardless and Cashfree, together with Stripe, PayPal and Razorpay. Each has a setup guide in
  [Connect a payment gateway](https://twominutebilling.com/help/guides/connect-a-payment-gateway).
- **More ways to pay.** Apple Pay, Google Pay, Venmo, Cash App Pay and PayPal through Braintree,
  plus direct debits such as Bacs, SEPA, ACH, BECS, PAD, Autogiro, Betalingsservice, PayTo, eNACH
  and UPI Autopay. Each payment shows the payment method that paid it.
- **The correct account for each payment.** With more than one gateway account, pay now and
  save a payment method each use an account that can do that action.
- **Gateway messages are not lost.** If we cannot process a message from your gateway, we try
  again for about four days. On **Gateway Webhooks**, select **Replay** to try again yourself.
- **Record a dispute.** If your gateway cannot report a chargeback, select **Record dispute** on
  the payment. Refunds that you make in your gateway now show in Two Minute Billing too.
- **Custom roles.** On **Team → Roles**, make a role with only the permissions that it needs.
  You can also limit an API key to the resources that it needs.
- **Safer API keys.** Each key shows when it was last used. Set an expiry date, or select
  **Rotate key** to replace a key with an overlap of up to 7 days.
- **Request logs.** **Developers → Request logs** shows each API request, with secrets removed.
  The webhook delivery log now has filters and paging.
- **Usage-based pricing.** Price usage as tiered, volume, stairstep, package or percentage, and
  set a minimum spend. Customers see their usage so far in the customer portal.
- **Usage on yearly plans.** Bill a yearly plan's usage each month, and set a minimum commitment
  for each term.
- **More control over collections.** Select **Exclude from dunning** for a customer, set a
  minimum amount for dunning in each currency, and give a customer their own dunning policy.
  Set how many days before a trial end, a renewal or a scheduled cancellation the reminder goes.
- **Receipts and payment requests.** Each payment gets a numbered receipt with a PDF, also in
  the customer portal. A payment request collects up to 50 open invoices in one charge.
- **HubSpot invoices.** Send your invoices to a custom object in HubSpot Enterprise.
- **More accurate bills.** Each billing period gets one invoice, credit notes reverse the
  correct tax, and a cancel at the end of a term bills the usage and charges of that term.

title: Check every change before you copy your set-up
summary: Copy set-up now shows each change first, copies your company profile and email sending, and keeps a list of past copies.
body:
**Copy set-up** (on the Transfer page) copies your configuration from one business to another.
Now you see each change before you copy, and you can copy more of your set-up.

- **Check the changes first.** Select **Check changes** to see each value that the copy changes,
  with its value now and its value after. Filter the list to new, replaced or left-out values.
  Secrets show as `••••`.
- **Leave out a section that cannot be copied.** If a section has a problem, the list tells you
  why. Select **Leave out these sections** to continue without it.
- **Copy your company profile.** Address, tax registration number, invoice issuer, default HSN/SAC
  code and default tax behavior.
- **Copy email sending.** Sender details and your SMTP or Amazon SES settings, with their secrets.
  Email templates stay with each business.
- **Keep each business's own numbers and links.** The destination keeps its invoice and credit
  note prefixes, its checkout return and cancel URLs and its portal error text. To give it new
  prefixes, enter them in the copy. The copy refuses a prefix that another business uses.
- **Start clean on a test business.** Select **Delete its catalog, coupons and taxes first** to
  give a test business an exact copy.
- **Copy the test businesses in the same run.** When you copy one live business to another, you
  can also copy their test businesses. The test businesses go first. If they fail, the live
  business does not change.

## Past copies

The **Past copies** list shows each copy for this business or for your whole organization, with
what it added and updated. Select **Repeat** to start a new copy with the same choices.

## Update a live business, with a confirmation

A live business takes only new records from a copy. To also change its settings, company
profile, email sending, numbering or tax profiles, an owner or admin selects **Also update what is
there** and types the business name to confirm. The audit log records each value that changed.
Invoices that you already issued keep their tax details.

title: Show a picture of each product
summary: Add an image to a product. Buyers see it on checkout, payment links, the pricing page and their purchases.
body:
Each product can now have an image. Buyers see it next to the product on the hosted checkout, on
payment links, on your pricing page and in their purchases in the customer portal.

- **Add an image.** On the new or edit page of a product, select an image: PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP,
  up to 5 MB. You see a preview before you save.
- **See what buyers see.** On a one-time product, the summary shows the product as the checkout
  shows it: the image, the name, the description and the price with its tax.
- **Send buyers to your page after payment.** Enter an **After-payment page**, for example a
  thank-you or download page. Checkout sends buyers there after they pay, if the checkout link or
  payment link has no page of its own.

## One-time products are easier to set up

- **How you sell it.** One card shows the two ways to sell a one-time product: on its own with a
  checkout link or payment link, or with a subscription, for example as a setup fee.
- **SKU and accounting codes.** Enter them with the first price.
- **Taxable.** Disable it for an item that has no tax, for example a gift card.
- **Next step.** After you create a one-time product, its page opens at its payment links.
- **Product ID.** If you leave the ID empty, we make one from the name.

title: Sell one-time products from the hosted checkout
summary: Sell setup fees, credit packs and other one-time products with a checkout link, a payment link or a pricing page.
body:
The hosted checkout now sells one-time products, not only subscriptions. When all the prices in a
checkout are one-time prices, the buyer pays once and gets a paid invoice. No subscription is
created. When a checkout has a recurring price, it continues to create a subscription.

- **One-time products.** The catalog shows them under **One-time products**. On a product page,
  the **Hosted checkout** card makes a checkout link for a one-time price.
- **Payment links.** Under **Payment links**, make one link that many buyers can use. Put it on
  your website or in an email. Each buyer gets their own checkout, customer record and invoice.
- **A public pricing page.** Show your products and prices on one page that buyers can open
  without a login.
- **Quantities.** On a payment link, you can let the buyer change the quantity, between the
  limits that you set.
- **Save the payment method.** In **Hosted pages → One-time purchases**, select if the checkout
  saves the buyer's payment method: never, always, or the buyer decides.

## A faster checkout

- **One page.** The buyer's details and the payment step show on one page. On a phone, the order
  lines fold to make the page shorter.
- **The total first.** The checkout shows the amount due today, with tax, before the buyer pays.
- **Faster to open.** The checkout loads the card form only when the buyer needs it.

## After the purchase

- **Purchases in the customer portal.** Buyers see their one-time purchases, each with a link to
  its receipt.
- **Payments that the bank must still confirm.** Sometimes a payment provider holds a payment to
  check it. We keep the payment and record it when the provider confirms it. In the customer
  portal, the buyer sees **Payment in progress**, and **Pay now** is not available for that
  invoice until the payment completes.

## Bring buyers back

- **Checkout reminders.** In **Emails**, switch on **Checkout reminder**. A buyer who gives an
  email address and does not complete the checkout gets a reminder after 1 hour, and a second
  reminder after 24 hours. The link in the email opens the same checkout. This email is off until
  you switch it on.
- **Two new reports.** In **Reports → Acquisitions**, **Checkout Reminders** shows how many buyers
  got a reminder and how many completed their checkout after it. **Recovered Checkout Revenue**
  shows the money from those purchases.

title: Each business has a live mode and a test mode
summary: Try your setup in the test mode of a business, then bill real customers in live mode.
body:
When you create a business, you get two modes: live and test. Live mode bills your real
customers. Use test mode to try your catalog, settings and integration before you go live.

- **One switch.** Inside a business, use **Mode** at the bottom of the navigation. You go to the
  same page in the other mode.
- **A copy to start.** Test mode starts with the settings of the live business. After that, the
  two modes are separate. A change in one mode does not change the other.
- **Move your setup.** To copy the catalog and settings from one mode to the other, use
  **Transfer & Sample Data**. The other mode of the business is already selected.
- **Two business IDs.** Each mode has its own business ID. A test API key gets access only to test
  mode, and a live API key gets access only to live mode. On the **Developers** page, your keys
  show in two groups: Live keys and Test keys.

## Safe to test

- **No real money.** Test mode uses the TM Billing Test Gateway. The hosted checkout and the
  customer portal show a "Test mode" notice.
- **Email only to your team.** In test mode, we send email only to the addresses of your team
  members. Other customer emails are not sent, and the email log shows why.
- **Start again.** In test mode, **Delete test data** deletes all customers and their
  subscriptions, invoices and payments. The catalog and settings stay.
- **HubSpot is live only.** Test data does not go into your CRM, so you connect HubSpot in live
  mode.

## Your existing businesses

Your organization overview and reports show live data. A business that you created before today
gets its test mode the first time that you select **Mode → Test**. Test businesses that you
created before today continue to work. The organization overview lists them separately.

title: A new account page, retention for your organization, and metadata rules
summary: Manage your profile and sessions, see retention for all businesses, and set and edit metadata with rules and suggestions.
body:
Your account shows your profile, appearance and security on one page.

- **Profile.** Enter your name and upload a profile photo. The sidebar and the Team list show them.
  If you sign in with Google and do not upload a photo, the dashboard shows your Google photo.
- **Appearance.** Select Light, Dark or System. The dashboard keeps your selection on all your
  browsers.
- **Active sessions.** See each browser where you are signed in and its last activity. Sign out
  one browser or all other browsers.

## Retention for your organization

The Performance card on the organization overview now shows the same rates as each business:
Quick ratio, Gross revenue retention, Net revenue retention and Customer churn. The organization
figures combine all your businesses in your reporting currency. A larger business has more effect
on the result than a smaller business. Each card shows the period that it measures.

## Rules for metadata

Set rules for the metadata on customers and subscriptions in **Settings → Metadata rules**.

- **Rules by path.** A rule applies to a key, or to a nested key such as `billing.po`. It sets the
  type of the value, and it can set a pattern, a maximum length or a list of permitted values.
- **Optional keys.** A rule examines a value only when the value is present. A missing key is
  always permitted.
- **On or off.** Validation is off until you enable it, separately for customers and for
  subscriptions. When it is on, the API and the dashboard refuse a value that does not obey a
  rule, and the error names the key.
- **Strict mode.** Enable strict mode to also refuse keys that do not have a rule.
- **Existing data stays.** Rules examine new and changed values only. Stored metadata does not
  change.
- **Number and list rules.** A number rule can permit only whole numbers and set a minimum and a
  maximum. A list rule can set the type of each item and the permitted item values.

## Edit metadata in a form

On a customer and on a subscription change, metadata is now a form, not a JSON text box.

- **A field for each rule.** A list of values shows as a menu or as buttons. A number shows as a
  number field. A nested key shows in a group. Errors show on the field before you save.
- **Key suggestions.** When you add a key, the form suggests the keys that your other customers or
  subscriptions use, with the number of records for each key. For a key with few values, the form
  also suggests the values.
- **Rules from your data.** In **Settings → Metadata rules**, the suggested keys have a **Create
  rule** button that fills in the rule for you.
- **JSON is still available.** Select **Edit as JSON** to edit the raw text.

## Search finds all pages

Push ⌘K (Ctrl K on Windows) and type the name of a page. All settings pages are in the search. This
includes dunning, email delivery, invoice settings, payment gateways and each billing rule. You can
also use common words. For example, "retries" finds dunning.

## On your phone

The account menu at the bottom of the navigation opens correctly. The navigation stays open below
the menu.

title: Two-factor authentication and passkeys for you and your team
summary: Protect each sign-in with an authenticator app or a passkey. Make it necessary for all your organization.
body:
Enable two-factor authentication on Your account. Then each sign-in asks for
a second proof. This applies when you sign in with a password and when you sign in with Google.

- **Passkeys.** Use your fingerprint, face or screen lock as the second step. You can also sign in
  with only a passkey. You do not type a password.
- **Authenticator apps.** Scan the QR code with an authenticator app. When you sign in, enter the
  6-digit code from the app. Each code operates one time only.
- **Recovery codes.** You get ten recovery codes. Each code operates one time only. Use a code if
  you lose your phone. You can download the codes and make a new set at any time.
- **Trusted browsers.** Select "Don't ask again on this browser" to skip the code for 30 days.
  When you change your password or disable two-factor authentication, the dashboard forgets all
  trusted browsers.

## Make two-factor authentication necessary for your organization

An admin can enable **Require two-factor authentication** in Settings.

- **Grace period.** Each teammate has seven days to enable two-factor authentication. The dashboard
  and an email remind them before the deadline.
- **Status of each teammate.** The Team list shows who has two-factor authentication, who must
  enable it, and the deadline.
- **API keys.** When this setting is on, only teammates with two-factor authentication can make
  new API keys. Existing keys continue to operate.

## You get an email for each security change

- **Security emails.** We send you an email when someone enables or disables two-factor authentication.
  We also send an email when you add or remove a method, use or replace recovery codes, or change
  your password.
- **Warning about your password.** Someone can enter your password correctly and then fail the
  second step many times. When this occurs, we send you an email. Change your password immediately.
- **If you cannot sign in.** On the code step, select "Get help signing in". Support can reset
  two-factor authentication after three days. We send you an email with a link. If you did not
  ask for the reset, use the link to cancel it.

title: Every record page, redesigned around what needs you
summary: Customers, subscriptions, invoices and the whole catalog open on what needs attention, then the numbers, then the detail.
body:
Every detail page now follows one layout: what needs your attention first, the key figures next,
then the record itself in clear sections. It applies to customers, subscriptions, invoices, credit
notes, transactions, payment intents, tax regions, products, prices, product groups,
coupons and coupon sets.

## Act on what needs you

- **Needs attention sits at the top.** An unpaid invoice shows how long it has been due, how many
  attempts were made and when the next retry is, with a timeline of every attempt and the retries
  still to come. Hover a step for the card and the decline reason.
- **Collect payment lets you choose.** On a customer, tick the unpaid invoices to collect; on an
  invoice or subscription, pick the card to charge. A payment you collect by hand never uses up
  one of the scheduled retries.
- **Invoices within their terms stay calm.** An invoice that is issued but not yet due is not
  flagged; Collect payment is still in More if a customer wants to pay early.

## Know your catalog

- **See what each plan earns.** Products, prices and product groups show their active
  subscriptions and MRR, per currency.
- **See what each coupon has given.** Coupons show every redemption and the total discount given;
  coupon sets show which subscription redeemed each code, can be renamed, and export their codes
  as CSV.
- **Limit redemptions per customer.** A coupon can now be capped at a number of uses per customer.
- **Activity and comments on catalog records.** Changes to products, prices, families, coupons and
  coupon sets appear in the Activity log, and your team can leave comments on them.

## Forms that preview the result

- **Create a plan with its price in one go.** New plans, add-ons and charges take their first price
  point on the same page, and every form shows a live summary such as "Customers pay $19.80 per seat
  every month, with a 14-day free trial."
- **Every option on one form.** Tiers, trials, billing cycles, tax behaviour and metadata are all
  editable where you create or edit the record. Fields that cannot change after creation say why.

## Easier to read

- **Long lists page instead of scrolling.** History, activity, comments, codes and redemptions show
  10 or 5 at a time, newest first, with every record reachable.
- **Tables keep their shape.** Columns stay fixed as rows appear, and long text wraps instead of
  pushing the table sideways.

title: Resuming a subscription bills exactly what it should
summary: A resume inside a paid term carries on at no charge; a resume after it starts and bills a new term.
body:
When you resume a paused subscription, what it bills now depends on one question: has the term
your customer already paid for ended?

- **Still inside the paid term:** the subscription carries on to the same renewal date and nothing
  new is charged. Your customer keeps the time they paid for.
- **After the paid term ended:** a new term starts on the day of the resume and is billed for in
  full, just like a renewal.

## Choose how the new term is billed

- **Invoice immediately** raises and collects the new term's invoice at the moment of resume.
  It is the default unless you have chosen otherwise.
- **Add to unbilled charges** holds the charge and bills it with the next invoice instead.
- **Set your default** in Settings → Billing rules → Pause and resume. The Resume dialog preselects
  it, and you can still pick the other option for a single resume.
- **The same rule applies everywhere:** resumes from the dashboard, the API, your customers'
  self-serve portal, and pauses that resume automatically after a set number of cycles.

title: Retries timed to when the payment is likely to go through
summary: With Smart decline handling, each retry can now be timed by why the payment failed, in your customer's morning.
body:
**Turn on Adaptive retry timing** in Settings → Dunning, alongside Smart decline handling. Instead
of one schedule for every failure, each retry is timed by the reason the payment was declined:

- **A gateway or network hiccup is retried within hours**, then after a day and after three days.
- **Insufficient funds is retried on the next likely payday**: the 1st, the 15th or the last day
  of the month, up to four times.
- **A generic decline is retried a few days apart**, then the invoice is held and your customer is
  asked to update their card.

## Retries land in your customer's morning

- **At 10:00 where the card was issued**, or in your business's timezone when that isn't known.
- **Card networks are respected.** When a card network or gateway says how long to wait before
  trying again, the next attempt waits at least that long.
- **Your limits still apply.** No retry lands more than 30 days after the due date or past your
  dunning period, and mandate debits (UPI, e-NACH, card mandates) keep your retry schedule.

These timings follow common practice rather than a guarantee, so compare your collections
recovery rate before and after you turn it on. Adaptive retry timing is off until you do, and
your existing schedule is unchanged.

## Also in this release, for every business

- **A card the network says not to retry is never charged again** until it's replaced or
  updated, including when you collect by hand. Retrying those cards can bring network fees.
- **Each card stays under the card networks' attempt limits.** When a card has been declined
  many times recently, across all its invoices, the next retry waits instead.

title: Dunning that reads why a payment failed
summary: Smart decline handling retries what can succeed, pauses what needs the customer, and keeps them informed until it is fixed.
body:
**Choose how failed payments are handled.** Settings → Dunning has a new **Decline handling**
option. _Fixed_ follows your retry schedule for every failure. _Smart_ reads the reason the
payment was declined and acts on it:

- **Temporary problems are retried**, such as insufficient funds or a bank that is briefly
  unavailable, on your schedule.
- **Problems only the customer can fix pause the invoice** instead of retrying a card that cannot
  succeed, such as an expired card or a cancelled mandate. Your customer is asked to update their
  payment method, and the invoice can be charged the moment they do.
- **Declines that must not be retried stop straight away**, such as a card reported lost or
  stolen.

## Customers hear from you while an invoice is paused

- **Reminders through the whole window.** A paused invoice gets a series of reminders spaced by
  your own retry schedule, each with an **Update payment method** button, so a new card settles
  this invoice and the next renewal too.
- **One last attempt before the deadline.** When the window closes, the invoice is charged once
  more before your final action runs.
- **Failure emails say when you will try again.** The payment failed email now shows the date of
  the next attempt.

## Also in this release

- **A customer with no payment method on file is given time to add one** instead of reaching
  your final action within days.
- **A problem with your own gateway account never cancels a customer.** Those invoices are paused
  rather than run to your final action, so you can fix the connection and collect.
- **Collections recovery rate** is a new measure you can add to any dashboard: of the invoices
  dunning finished with, the share it recovered. It counts from today.

title: Reports you can build on, and a history you can trust
summary: A full reports section, boards you arrange yourself, saved segments, and past figures stated exactly as they were on the day.
body:
**Reports** is now its own section: close to a hundred reports across recurring revenue, customers,
billing, cash, receivables, tax and collections, with charts, breakdowns and CSV export.

## Boards you arrange

- **Start from a built-in board** — five of them, so the section is useful on day one.
- **Build your own** by adding widgets: pick a type (a single figure, a ranked breakdown or a
  table), the measure, and how to split it, over a preset or custom period.
- **Compare with the previous period** on any figure, in every currency the business bills in.

## Segments

- **Save a group of customers as a segment** and ask MRR, its movements or customer counts
  for just that group.
- **Split a figure by country or plan** to see which part of the book moved it.

## A history you can trust

- **Past MRR is what each subscription actually earned that day.** An upgrade, a discount or a
  reactivation lands on the day it happened, and every earlier day keeps the figure it had.
- **A trial counts once it converts**, and a cancelled account keeps the rate it was paying
  until the day it left.
- **Movements add up.** New, expansion, reactivation, contraction and churn sum exactly to the
  change in MRR, month after month.

## Every currency, at the rate of the day

- **Converted figures use the exchange rate that applied on the day**, from the European Central
  Bank's daily reference rates, so a figure from two years ago is stated at that year's rate.
- **Currency moves have their own line** in the MRR movement report, so a weaker or stronger
  currency never reads as growth or churn.

## Faster, and easier to find

- **The business home answers one period on every tab**, with eight presets and a custom range.
- **Subscriptions read as Active, Paying and Renewing** — everything live, what carries revenue,
  and what is set to renew — side by side on both homes, with a Renewing report of its own.
- **See collections at a glance**: the business home shows how many invoices are in dunning, and
  the businesses list has a Dunning column.
- **Reports and the business home load faster** on large books.
- **The organization sidebar lists your businesses**, so you can jump straight to one.

title: Delete a subscription
summary: Remove a subscription that should never have been there, and keep every invoice it raised.
body:
A subscription created by mistake — a duplicate, a test, an import that went wrong — can now be
deleted. Open it and use **Delete subscription** in the actions rail, or call
`DELETE /v1/businesses/{business}/subscriptions/{subscription}`.

- **The billing stops and the books stay.** The subscription leaves your lists and its page, and
  nothing renews it again. Its invoices, payments and credit notes are kept exactly as they were and
  stay on the customer, so your revenue history reads the same after the delete as before it.
- **Anything still owed is still owed.** An unpaid invoice raised by a deleted subscription remains
  payable and keeps running through dunning — deleting the subscription does not write off the debt.
- **Deleting is not cancelling, and the dialog says so.** There is no final invoice, no credit for
  unused time and no cancellation on the record. If you want the term closed out properly, cancel
  the subscription instead; delete is for the one that should not exist at all.

Deleting is available to managers and owners, and every delete is recorded in the audit log with who
did it. Integrations can listen for the new `subscription_deleted` event.

title: Open a charge in your gateway, from the transaction
summary: The gateway transaction id on a transaction is now a link straight to that charge on Stripe, Razorpay or PayPal, in the right mode.
body:
Reconciling a payment no longer means copying an id into your gateway's search box.

- **The gateway transaction id links to the charge.**
  On a transaction, the id the provider gave the charge opens that charge on the provider's own
  dashboard in a new tab — Stripe, Razorpay and PayPal.
- **The transactions list carries it too.**
  A new **Gateway Charge Id** column sits beside Gateway, linked the same way, so you can jump to
  the provider without opening each transaction first. Hide it from the column chooser if you would
  rather not see it.
- **It opens in the right mode.**
  A test charge opens the provider's test dashboard or sandbox and a live one opens live, so the
  link never lands on an account where the charge does not exist.
- **Ids with nowhere to go stay plain text.**
  Simulated and offline payments have no gateway page, and a refund is reached through the payment
  it reverses — those ids are shown as before rather than as links that would go nowhere.

title: Know the card before you charge it
summary: Every payment method now shows where it was issued, who issued it and what it can do — the same way on the customer and the subscription.
body:
A saved payment method now tells you everything the gateway knows about it, and it tells you the
same story wherever you open it.

- **Where the card was issued, and by whom.** The issuing country and the issuing bank sit on the
  instrument. For Indian-issued cards that is what decides whether a renewal has to ask the payer
  to authenticate, so it is worth seeing before the renewal runs rather than after.
- **What the instrument can actually do.** Funding type (credit, debit, prepaid), consumer or
  business, 3D Secure support, international use, and whether it can be debited off-session at
  all. A card that cannot take recurring debits says so next to the mandate riding on it.
- **A fingerprint, where the gateway provides one.** The same underlying card can be saved twice
  under different tokens; the fingerprint is how you tell that a backup is really a second card.

## One card, both screens

The payment method on a customer and the payment method on a subscription are drawn by the same
component now, so they carry the same rows in the same order and read the same at a glance.

- **A subscription that charges its own card says so in words.** The line under the heading tells
  you whether the instrument is set on this subscription or is the customer's primary, and the
  badge beside it keeps its plain meaning: the customer's primary card.
- **UPI Autopay looks like UPI.** A mandate with no card brand now carries its own mark instead of
  a generic card.
- **The detail grid follows the space it is given**, so a long gateway reference stays readable in
  a narrow column instead of breaking across half a dozen lines.

## Two roles, one word for each

A saved card had three words — primary, backup and default — for two roles, and which word you saw
depended on which screen you were on. There are two roles, and they are now called the same thing
everywhere: in your dashboard, in your customer's billing portal, at checkout, and in the API.

- **The primary card is charged first.** What used to read _default_ in the portal and at checkout
  now reads _primary_, matching your dashboard and the `role` field on the API.
- **The backup is tried only when the primary fails**, and only when it is genuinely a different
  card. It now pairs with a word that has an opposite.
- The customer's payment methods panel says this once, above the cards, so the roles need no
  explanation — and a support conversation no longer needs translating between two screens.

Nothing changed about how collection behaves, and the API keeps `is_default` and the
`/payment_methods/:id/default` route exactly as they were, so existing integrations are unaffected.

Instruments saved before we began asking gateways for these details will show _Not reported_ for
the issuing country — an honest blank rather than a guess.

title: A customer's whole history, on the customer
summary: The customer page now shows everything that happened to that customer — renewals, invoices, payments, credit notes — as well as the raw event stream.
body:
Open a customer and you can see their whole life with you, not just the edits made to their
record.

- **The Activity log covers everything the customer owns.**
  Renewals, invoices raised and paid, payments and refunds, credit notes and payment-method
  changes all appear alongside the changes made to the customer itself — each row naming the
  record it is about, who did it, and where from.
- **The Events tab is back, scoped the same way.**
  The developer's view of the same history: event id, type, the record it names, its source and
  when it happened — the list you reach for when you are matching a webhook to what the engine
  actually did.
- **Both read the whole footprint.**
  Subscriptions, invoices, credit notes, transactions, payments, refunds and saved payment
  methods — one customer, one history.

## For API users

`GET /v1/businesses/:business/events` and `GET /v1/businesses/:business/audit_logs` take a
`customer=<id>` parameter that scopes either stream to everything that customer owns, so you no
longer have to fan out over their records and merge the results yourself.

title: Pay another way, without the risk of paying twice
summary: The portal offers a second way to pay only where the first attempt can actually be stopped, and payment records now say what the gateway said.
body:
A customer waiting on a bank approval can pay another way — where we can safely stop the
first attempt.

- **"Pay now" appears only when the first attempt can be cancelled.**
  Some banks can authorise a payment retroactively, for up to three days, with nothing for
  the cardholder to decline. Where that is possible, we no longer offer a second route that
  could take the money twice; the invoice waits instead.
- **The confirmation says what will happen.**
  Before anything is released, your customer is told plainly that we will cancel the bank's
  request, and to decline it if it still reaches them.
- **Payment records carry the gateway's own answer.**
  Whether a payment is waiting on the cardholder is taken from what the gateway states, and
  a later statement replaces an earlier one — so a record never keeps saying "no approval
  needed" after the gateway has asked for approval.
- **A quiet payment is no longer read as a stalled one.**
  Time alone never decides that a customer has been asked to authenticate.
- **Approval is asked for on Indian cards, where the rule applies.**
  The RBI mandate rules follow the card's issuing country, not the currency, so a foreign
  card paying in rupees is treated as what it is.

## Payment methods know more about themselves

- **Every saved method records its issuing country, funding type, bank and capabilities.**
  Cards, netbanking, UPI, wallets and direct debits all carry the same facts, so routing and
  retries can use them. Card numbers are never stored.
- **Re-adding a card updates the one you already have.**
  Saving the same card again keeps the existing method and its history instead of leaving a
  duplicate behind.
- **A backup payment method has to be a different card.**
  If your backup turns out to be the same card as the primary, it is no longer used as a
  fallback — retrying the same card against the same decline never helped anyone.

title: Refresh a screen without losing your place
summary: Every list and the invoice, subscription, transaction and customer screens now reload the numbers on demand — keeping your filters, your sort and your scroll exactly as they were.
body:
Billing moves while you are looking at it: the clock issues invoices, gateways answer
minutes later, and payers act in their own portal. Every screen that shows that kind of
state now has a Refresh control that fetches the current answer on the spot.

- **Your view survives a refresh.** Refresh re-runs the search, filters, segment and sort
  you already have applied, so a narrowed list comes back narrowed. It reloads the rows
  and nothing else — the page does not reload and you do not return to the top.
- **On a list, one control covers everything you monitor.** Invoices, Transactions,
  Subscriptions, Customers, Credit notes, Payment intents, Events, Retries, Emails,
  Gateway requests, Gateway webhooks, the Audit log and Ops due-work all carry it.
- **On a record, only what moves gets fetched.** Open an invoice and Refresh brings its
  status, amount due, payments, credits and retry schedule up to date; the line items,
  addresses and tax stay put. Subscriptions refresh their status, term and next billing;
  transactions their settlement and refunds; customers their balance, credits and payment
  methods.
- **On a transaction, Refresh and Sync are different questions.** Refresh shows what we
  already know. Sync goes and asks the gateway. Both are available and neither pretends to
  be the other.
- **The business dashboard says when it last synced, and lets you do something about it.**
  The freshness of the figures is now next to the control that updates them.

title: India auto-debits ask only when the bank asks
summary: A recurring payment that is only waiting on its pre-debit notification now reads as in progress, not as something your customer has to approve.
body:
An India e-mandate payment now says exactly what it is waiting for.

Under RBI rules every e-mandate debit pauses briefly while the pre-debit notification goes
out to the cardholder. Most of those debits need nothing from anyone — the notification is
served, the charge presents itself, and the money arrives. Some genuinely do need the
cardholder to authenticate. Your customers now only hear from us about the second kind.

- **The portal asks for approval only when approval is actually required.**
  A payment waiting on nothing but its notification window shows as in progress, so nobody
  is prompted to act on a charge that will complete on its own.
- **Payment records name the kind of wait.**
  Whether an attempt is waiting on the bank's notification or on the cardholder is taken
  from what the gateway states, not inferred from the amount — so the Retries and payment
  screens agree with the gateway.
- **Every amount is treated the same way.**
  An auto-debit is not assumed to be unattended just because it is small, and not assumed
  to need authentication just because it is large.
- **A charge above the approved limit can now be authorised in one step.**
  When a renewal exceeds the per-charge limit on an Indian card mandate, the bank offers the
  cardholder a link to approve that single payment. They now get it, instead of being asked
  to set up their auto-debit again from scratch.
- **When a bank asks us to wait, we wait.**
  A decline that comes back with "try again in 24 hours" no longer spends a retry the same
  night on an attempt the network has already said it will refuse.

title: A transaction says where it came from
summary: Open a charge and you can see the authentication it came through and whatever the gateway has said about fraud.
body:
A transaction now names the authorization behind it, and carries the gateway's own fraud verdict — both on the page you were already looking at.

- **Follow a charge back to its payment intent.** Where a customer authenticated — a checkout, a portal payment, an operator collecting an invoice — the transaction links straight to that intent and its attempts. You could always walk from the intent to the charge; now it goes both ways.
  Renewals show no link, and that is the honest answer: nobody is present to authenticate an automatic renewal, so no intent is ever created for one.
- **See a fraud warning where the money is.** If the card network flags a charge as probably fraudulent, or the gateway puts it under manual review, the transaction says so and when it was reported.
  It sits alongside the charge's own status rather than replacing it, so you can always still tell whether the money settled.

## Developers

`payment_intent` and `fraud_signal` are new on the transaction object. Both are nullable, `fraud_signal` is served on the single-transaction read, and both are in the OpenAPI spec and the generated SDK.

title: Retries and Disputes sit with your work, not your logs
summary: Money at risk is on the sidebar with a live count, Billing LogIQ is now Billing rules, and a payment intent links to the transactions it produced.
body:
The two screens that track money you can still lose now sit in the sidebar alongside
Customers and Subscriptions.

- **Retries carries a live count.** The number of invoices the billing clock is still
  working on shows on the sidebar from every page, so revenue in dunning is something you
  see rather than something you go looking for.
- **Disputes has its own place.** A chargeback runs against an evidence deadline, so it is
  no longer filed with webhook payloads.
- **Every dispute is reachable.** The disputes API now reports how many there are and pages
  through all of them, and the screen says so plainly when it is showing only the most
  recent ones.
- **"Billing LogIQ" is now "Billing rules."** The same nine settings — billing mode,
  payment terms, proration, round-off and the subscription-change rules — under a name that
  says what they do. Existing links and bookmarks redirect on their own.
- **A payment intent links to the money it moved.** Open an intent and jump straight to its
  transactions, so an authentication step and the charge that followed read as one story.

title: Choose what customers can do in the portal
summary: Three new switches on Hosted pages decide whether customers can download invoices, pay them, and remove a saved payment method.
body:
Settings → Hosted pages has a new section: **What customers can do in the portal**. Three
switches, all on unless you turn them off, so nothing changes until you decide it should.

- **Let customers download their invoices.** Turning it off keeps the invoice visible — a
  customer still sees what they were billed — but removes the PDF download.
- **Let customers pay an unpaid invoice.** This removes the customer's own Pay now only. We
  still collect on your schedule and dunning still runs, so turning it off does not stop the
  money arriving. Useful if you collect strictly by mandate or bank transfer and a second,
  manual path would muddle your reconciliation.
- **Let customers remove a payment method.** Adding one is always allowed; this governs
  removal. Worth turning off where a live subscription depends on the card or mandate on
  file — nothing else prevents a customer removing it.
- **Let customers pause or resume their own subscription.** Turning it off keeps the subscription active
  even if the customer would like to cancel. Worth turning off where a live subscription depends on
  the customer's subscription — nothing else prevents a customer canceling it.
- **Let customers cancel their own subscription.** Turning it off keeps the subscription active
  even if the customer would like to cancel. Worth turning off where a live subscription depends on
  the customer's subscription — nothing else prevents a customer canceling it.

Each switch applies to the self-serve portal only, and takes effect immediately for every
customer of that business.

title: Upload your logo instead of hosting it
summary: Pick a file on Brand styles or Documents and we store it — no public URL to arrange first.
body:
Your logo, icon, favicon and invoice signature can now be uploaded straight from settings. Choose
a file and it is stored and served for you, so branding your invoices, checkout, portal and email
no longer waits on somewhere to host an image.

- **Upload or paste — both still work.** The URL field stays exactly where it was, so an image you
  already host anywhere public needs no change.
- **PNG or JPEG for anything that prints, up to 5 MB.** Your logo and signature are embedded in
  invoice PDFs, so those two take PNG or JPEG; icons and favicons also take GIF and WebP. We read
  the file itself to decide what it is rather than trusting its name, so a mislabelled file is
  caught before it reaches your customers.
- **Two places to do it.** Your logo, icon and favicon live on Settings → Brand styles; the
  signature that prints on invoices and credit notes lives on Settings → Documents.
- **Using an SVG today? Upload a PNG or JPEG to see it on your invoices.** Invoice PDFs carry
  PNG and JPEG; an SVG still shows on your portal, checkout and email, but the PDF prints your
  business name in place of the mark. Uploading takes a few seconds and fixes it everywhere.

Every surface that shows your brand — the self-serve portal, hosted checkout, invoice PDFs and
billing email — picks up the new image as soon as you save.

title: Decide what goes on your invoices
summary: Line items now show units and unit price, and you choose your invoice title, number format, which fields appear, your address layout and a signature.
body:
Your invoices and credit notes now follow your rules. Pick what they're called, how they're
numbered, which fields they carry, and sign them off.

- **Call it what your tax authority expects.** Invoices can print as `INVOICE` or `TAX INVOICE`;
  credit notes as `CREDIT NOTE` or `REFUND`. Settings → Invoices, and Settings → Credit notes.
- **Number them your way.** Add a date stamp to the number — the year, the fiscal year, a month or
  a full date, in thirteen formats — choose the separators, and set how far the counter steps. The
  screen shows you the actual next number as you type, so you can see the result before you save.
  The counter always moves forward, so changing the format is safe.
- **Show only the fields you want.** Customer ID, subscription ID, billing address and tax number,
  invoice status, billing period, next billing date. Plus three you can now switch **on**: the
  shipping address, the credit notes raised against an invoice, and up to three of your own custom
  fields.
- **Lay out your address to suit your letterhead.** Expanded over several lines, collapsed to one,
  or a template you write yourself — previewed with your own address in it.
- **Sign your documents.** Add a signature line and an image, and choose which bottom corner they
  sit in — bottom right or bottom left. The block is pinned to the foot of the page, so it lands in
  the same place whether the invoice has two lines or twenty. Settings → Documents.
- **Tell offline payers where to send the money.** Build bank transfer or PayPal blocks with your
  own labels and values, and print them on your invoices. You can match them to the invoice
  currency or the customer's country, so a customer paying in euros isn't shown your rupee account.
  Settings → Payment instructions.

**Your line items now show their maths.** Every invoice gains a **Units** and a **Unit price**
column, so a line reads `5 × ₹940.00 = ₹4,700.00` instead of just the total. Nothing to switch on —
it is on every invoice and credit note from now on.

Everything else about your existing documents is untouched until you change something. Every setting starts at exactly
what your invoices already do, so nothing shifts under you the day this arrives.

One correction worth calling out: a tax registration number was previously labelled "GSTIN" on
every invoice, whichever country you sell from. It now says GSTIN in India, VAT across the EU and
the UK, and "Tax ID" elsewhere — so if you sell outside India, that caption on your documents is
now the right one.

title: ⌘K finds a customer by phone or company
summary: Quick search matches every field it says it does, across every row — not just the page in front of it.
body:
Press ⌘K inside a business, type whatever you remember about a record, and it comes back.

- **Phone and company find a customer.** Quick search matches the same fields the customer
  list does — id, email, first and last name, company and phone — so the thing you happen to
  have in front of you is enough to find the account.
- **Subscriptions and invoices search the whole list**, however long it has grown, and return
  the closest five of each alongside the customers.
- **A search in progress says so.** The palette reads "Searching…" while it is looking, and
  only reports nothing found once it knows.

title: Every payment attempt is on the record
summary: Whatever the gateway answers, the attempt and its reason land in tmbilling where you can see them.
body:
Every charge now leaves a trail you can read, whichever way it was started — the billing clock
renewing, an operator pressing **Collect now**, or the payer pressing **Pay now** in the portal.

- A charge the gateway turns down writes a **payment attempt** carrying the gateway's own wording,
  so the reason an invoice is still unpaid is on the screen next to it.
- Attempts appear in the customer's **Transactions** and on the invoice itself.
- Charges the gateway accepts but that never complete are picked up by the sweep, across every
  gateway you have connected.
- An instrument that is not authorised for the amount is caught before the charge goes out, so the
  payer gets a clear answer instead of a gateway error.

## Your gateway statement says which flow charged

A renewal, an operator collecting early, and a payer paying themselves all reach the gateway the
same way. Every charge tmbilling sends now carries a description naming the flow it came from, so a
line in your Stripe or RazorPay dashboard can be explained without opening tmbilling beside it.

title: Two dunning settings, and open checkouts on the invoice
summary: Retry behaviour and end-of-dunning behaviour are set separately, and an invoice shows the checkout waiting at the gateway.
body:
**Dunning is two settings now.** What happens while an invoice is being retried and what happens
when retries run out are separate choices, so you can keep collecting without committing to what
happens at the end — and change one without disturbing the other.

**An invoice shows the checkout that is open at the gateway.** When a payer has a hosted checkout
session waiting, the invoice says so, so you can tell "nobody has tried" apart from "somebody is
part-way through". A payment intent that is no longer wanted can be voided from the same place.

**The dunning card names the final attempt.** Before it happens, the screen tells you what the last
attempt will do, so the end of a dunning cycle holds no surprises.

title: Forms, search and loading states
summary: Saved values stay saved, search keeps up on long lists, and each page's loading state matches the page.
body:
- **A saved form shows the saved values.** Save a form and what you see is what was written, straight
  away.
- **Search keeps up.** Typing in a list filter now only re-renders what actually changed, so long
  tables stay responsive as you type.
- **Loading states match their page.** Each screen's placeholder now has the shape of the screen that
  is coming — a table where a table is coming, sections where sections are coming — so it tells you
  where to look.
- **Organization screens follow your time zone.** System, Audit Log and Developers render timestamps
  in the display time zone you set, alongside every other date.
- **Reason codes, custom fields and error handling** read cleanly, and the decline-rules table now
  matches the density of every other list.

title: A new look for the dashboard
summary: Cards on a tinted ground, one accent colour, and colour reserved for the rows that need you.
body:
The dashboard has a visual direction of its own.

- **Cards sit on a tinted ground.** Every panel, table and form reads as a distinct surface, which
  makes a long page much easier to scan.
- **One accent colour** carries both links and the primary action on a screen, so what to do next is
  always obvious.
- **Colour means something.** A state that needs a human — payment due, failed — keeps a filled
  badge. Healthy and finished states render quiet, so a list of mostly-cancelled subscriptions reads
  calm rather than alarming.
- **Softer corners, roomier rows, and a 12px floor on type**, so nothing on a screen you read all day
  is smaller than that.
- **Charts follow the theme**, in light and dark.

## The sidebar collapses

The navigation rail shrinks to an icon strip and remembers your choice, giving wide tables back
around 240px. Press the handle on its edge to switch.

title: The Retries screen shows what will actually be retried
summary: Only invoices with a live retry schedule appear, and an invariant watches for bills nobody will collect.
body:
The **Retries** screen lists the invoices the billing clock is genuinely still working on, so its
count is a number you can act on rather than a backlog to interpret.

Alongside it, a new invariant watches for the opposite case — an invoice that will never be
collected by anyone — and surfaces it rather than leaving it to be discovered.

Both feed the same goal: the screens that say "money is still coming" should only ever list money
that is still coming.

title: The invoice document, rebuilt
summary: Clearer hierarchy, a readable line-item table, correct billing periods, and the invoice can be issued by the organization.
body:
The invoice PDF and its on-screen version were rebuilt: clearer hierarchy, a readable line-item
table, totals that add up in front of you, and tax presented the way the place of supply requires.

- **Every invoice states the period it covers**, read from the lines it was billed for — so a
  historical invoice reads as a record of its own period.
- **An invoice can be issued by the organization** rather than a single business, for merchants who
  bill under one legal entity.
- **Countries print as names**, and the document offers what a finance team expects to find on it.
- **Logos reach the PDF**, including SVG.

title: Decide how each gateway decline behaves
summary: A screen for every decline code your gateways can return — what it means, whether we retry it, and what the payer is told.
body:
Gateways speak in error codes, and each one deserves a different answer: retry this one tomorrow,
never retry that one, tell the payer to call their bank. **Error handling** is a screen for exactly
that.

- **Every code we recognise is listed**, not only the ones you have already seen, so you can decide
  in advance rather than after a failed renewal.
- **Codes are grouped**, with the wording the payer will read shown beside each.
- **A business can override any rule** — set an error code's behaviour once and it applies to every
  future decline of that code.
- **RazorPay merchants see RazorPay's codes**, and the network's own do-not-retry instruction is
  respected where the network sends one.
- The same rules are available on the API: list them, and change how one decline behaves for a
  business.

title: Payment methods show their own card marks
summary: Operator screens show the real network mark — the same one the payer sees in the portal.
body:
A payer finds their card by its logo, not by re-reading four digits. Operator screens now do the
same: a Visa, a RuPay card, a UPI Autopay mandate and a bank debit are each recognisable at a
glance — which is exactly what you want on the screens where a failed payment gets triaged.

The mark comes from the same place the storefront uses, so the payer and the operator are always
looking at the same thing.

**Pay now works for cards vaulted on any gateway.** Routing follows the instrument that will actually
be charged, so a customer paying in INR with a card vaulted on Stripe pays without a detour.

title: Ask the gateway about a stuck payment
summary: A read-only check that fetches what the gateway currently knows, and shows you the answer.
body:
When a payment has been sitting in an unclear state, you can now ask the gateway directly. The
transaction shows a **check now** control that fetches the gateway's current view and displays it
beside ours.

- It is a **read**. Checking never moves money and never spends a retry.
- The panel names the actual gateway, and says plainly when nothing has changed yet rather than
  implying a result.
- The gateway's answer is shown as the gateway gave it, so there is nothing to take on trust.

title: Reactivation rules, and a mandate warning before you commit
summary: Choose whether reactivation requires a payment, and see at create time whether the mandate can carry the amount.
body:
**Reactivation is configurable.** Whether bringing a cancelled subscription back requires a successful
payment first is now a setting, so the rule can match how you actually sell.

**A mandate limit is flagged at create time.** When a subscription's amount would exceed what the
customer's mandate is authorised to carry, the create screen says so — while it is still a decision,
rather than at the first renewal.

The reactivation preview also shows the same totals the invoice will carry, so the number you approve
is the number that gets billed.

title: Pending debits stay pending, and mandates travel with the card
summary: An off-session bank debit is reported as in-flight until it settles, and the stored mandate is sent with the charge.
body:
- **An off-session debit that is still in flight is reported as pending**, not as a failure — so it
  is left to settle, and the payer is charged exactly once.
- **A stored mandate is sent with the charge.** Where the gateway issued one, tmbilling presents it,
  which is what keeps recurring debits authorised.
- **Voiding an invoice returns its credit**, and a parked invoice can close, so nothing stays
  reserved against a bill that no longer exists.
- **Cancellation credit is calculated from the current term**, so the amount you are shown at cancel
  time is the amount that is issued.

title: Direct debit and wallets on Stripe
summary: Bank debit rails and wallet payments are reachable, with recovery paths of their own.
body:
Stripe **direct debit** and **wallet** payments are now reachable from checkout and the portal, so
buyers who do not want to hand over a card have a route that works.

- **Direct-debit rails have their own failure and recovery handling**, because a bank debit fails
  differently from a card and deserves a different answer.
- **A paused mandate is re-asked.** When a mandate can no longer carry a charge, the payer is invited
  to re-authorise rather than the payment simply not happening.
- **A vaulted method's mandate can be recovered from the gateway**, so a method that arrived through
  a migration is as usable as one created here.

title: India mandate ceilings, and credit that stays visible
summary: The mandate ceiling is set where the gateway reads it, and a customer's credit stays visible after cancellation.
body:
- **The India card-mandate ceiling is set on the intent**, which is where the gateway reads it — so
  the amount a mandate is authorised for is the amount that gets registered, and the same card gets
  the same answer every time.
- **Credit stays visible after a cancellation.** Money you owe a customer remains on their page
  whatever happened to the subscription that produced it.
- **PayPal refunds are tagged**, so a refund can be traced back to the payment it reverses.
- **Holds that never captured no longer book a reversal**, keeping the ledger a record of money that
  actually moved.

title: Alerts that name the rows they counted
summary: Every alert links to the exact rows behind its number, and operational noise is separated from correctness.
body:
An alert that says "37" and stops there costs you the next ten minutes. Every alert now **names the
rows it counted** and links straight to them, with the filters already applied.

- **Operations and correctness are separate.** Something slow or retrying is a different kind of news
  from something that does not add up, and they no longer share a list.
- **A warning that will not clear escalates.** A condition that persists gets louder instead of
  staying at the same level indefinitely.
- **Gateway money is legible.** The screens that reconcile what the gateway holds against what we
  booked now show which captures are ours and what each one belongs to.
- **A possible double charge is called what it is**, so the most expensive thing to miss is the
  clearest thing on the screen.

title: Simpler sign-in, and a webhook resend that shows its exchange
summary: Fewer password prompts, Google sign-in on an invite, and a resend that shows the request and response live.
body:
## Signing in

- **Fewer password re-prompts.** Being signed in is enough for the things that only needed proof you
  were signed in.
- **Google sign-in works from an invite**, so a new teammate can accept and be working in one step.
- **A signed-in visitor who lands on the sign-in page is sent onward**, and signing in returns you to
  the page you were heading for rather than the home page.

## Webhooks

**Resend calls your endpoint immediately and shows the exchange** — the request we sent and the
response you returned, on screen, while you watch. Endpoints can be named when you create them, and
the delivery log groups one card per endpoint so a noisy endpoint is easy to find.

title: The billing clock got faster
summary: Settlement sweeps were the bulk of every cycle; they are now a small part of it.
body:
Settlement sweeps accounted for the overwhelming majority of each billing tick. They have been
scoped to the work that actually needs doing, which gives every cycle back to the work you care
about — renewals, retries and invoicing.

The practical effect: the clock keeps up comfortably at your current book size, with room as it
grows.

title: Exchange rates refresh themselves
summary: Daily rates from the ECB, stamped onto each invoice at issue time — and next renewal's tax on the subscription.
body:
**Rates refresh daily from the European Central Bank**, so a multi-currency book converts at
something current without anyone maintaining a table.

**Each invoice stamps the rate it was issued at.** A converted amount on an invoice stays the amount
that was invoiced, whatever rates do afterwards — which is what makes the document a record rather
than a live calculation.

**The subscription page shows next renewal's tax**, so the amount the customer will be charged is
visible before it happens rather than after.

title: The billing clock has a diary
summary: A due-date index you can read, maintained as work is scheduled — plus fair scheduling across tenants.
body:
**`/ops/due-work` is the billing clock's diary.** Everything the clock is going to do, when it is
going to do it, and what is overdue — on one screen, readable at a glance.

- The diary is **maintained as work is written**, so it is accurate the moment you open it rather
  than as of the last sweep.
- **The tick's pass list is declared and enforced**, so what the clock does each cycle is a stated
  contract rather than an emergent one.
- **No tenant can starve another.** Work is scheduled fairly across businesses, so one large book
  does not delay everyone else's renewals.
- A healthy tick is reported as healthy, so the alerts that fire are the ones worth reading.
